summary: Aluni is an open source crop rotation assistant that turns NASA Earth observations into a plain, field-level comparison a farmer can read on a phone. The farmer drops a pin on a map and answers five short questions. Aluni then pulls 20 years of climate (NASA POWER), vegetation (Landsat NDVI), slope (NASADEM), extreme rain (GPM IMERG) and soil moisture (SMAP) for that exact field. It compares the current rotation against at least three alternatives (adding a legume, a small grain, a different crop family or perennial forage) over three seasons. Each strategy gets a score from 0 to 100 on seven criteria, weighted by the farmer's own goals, and lists its evidence, benefits, gaps and risks. A month-by-month timeline shows when soil would be bare during storm, drought, frost or heat periods and proposes a cover crop for each exposed window. This matters because climate risk is rising and rotation choices compound over seasons. Free NASA data rarely reaches small and Spanish-speaking farmers. Aluni is live at aluni.us in English and Spanish, with passkey sign-in and accessibility options. It supports the farmer's judgment instead of replacing it.
details:
What it does and how it works
Aluni is a web and mobile app that helps farmers choose crop rotations using NASA data about their own field. The loop is simple. The farmer drops a pin and answers five essential questions: the pin, watering, current crop, past seasons and up to three goals. Then they open “Your plan”, follow the season with forecasts and alerts, and record the harvest so next season’s plan recomputes.

  • “Your plan”: the current rotation compared with legume, small-grain, other-family and perennial-forage strategies over three seasons. Each one is scored 0–100 on seven criteria (crop fit, pest break, soil health, nitrogen, water, erosion and workload). The farmer’s goals weigh their criteria three times.
  • Three-season exposure timeline: marks bare months under storm, dry, frost and heat bands and proposes a cover crop for each exposed window.
  • “Your field from space”: 20 years of climate, soil, slope, monthly NDVI and bare-soil periods. Every value is labelled with the dataset that measured it.
  • Follow-up tools: 7-day forecast, daily frost, heat, heavy-rain and dry-spell alerts, reports, and CSV/JSON export.
  • Sonda field station (designed): a solar soil and weather sensor that will put ground readings next to SMAP, IMERG and NASA POWER for the same pin.

Benefits
It is free and open source and runs on about $0 of hosting. Sign-in uses passkeys (face or fingerprint) instead of passwords. Only the pin is required to start. Every number shows its source, and every strategy lists its gaps and risks. Coverage is global, with richer layers in the US. The app is bilingual (English/Spanish) and accessible from the first screen.

Intended impact

  • Less exposed soil, and therefore less erosion, by flagging bare months under storm or drought and proposing cover crops.
  • Better use of water and nitrogen by comparing crop water need with local rain and counting legume seasons.
  • Fewer surprise losses thanks to daily weather alerts.
  • NASA evidence within reach of small and Spanish-speaking farmers, who usually cannot pay advisers.
  • Better conversations with extension agents: a “Talk this over with your adviser” list gives each farmer concrete questions.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: Ruby 4.0, Rust 1.92, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Swift, Kotlin.
  • Backend: Ruby on Rails 8.1, PostgreSQL 16, Redis 7, Sidekiq 8, plus a Rust extension for heavy calculations.
  • Frontend: Hotwire (Turbo, Stimulus), pure CSS, Three.js, and Leaflet with OpenStreetMap.
  • Mobile: Hotwire Native for iOS and Android.
  • AI: Google Gemini on Vertex AI, capped at 2000 requests/day. It only narrates facts the rules already computed.
  • Hosting: Google Compute Engine, Kamal 2, Cloudflare Tunnel and GitHub Actions.
  • Testing: RSpec, Cuprite, RuboCop, Brakeman.
  • Hardware (designed): ESP32-S3, Quectel BG95-M3 LTE-M/GNSS, ATECC608B secure element, capacitive soil probes, SHT45, rain gauge, 5 W solar panel and LiFePO4 battery.

How it is creative

  • Aluni, a 3D seedling mascot, guides the farmer, so the app feels like a helper instead of a form.
  • Satellite data is told as the story of one field, not as regional charts.
  • The exposure timeline shows when soil is vulnerable and how to protect it.
  • AI is used with guardrails: Gemini explains but cannot invent numbers.
  • Passkeys replace passwords, which is rare in agricultural software.

Factors the team considered

  • Farmer autonomy: the tool compares and explains, and the farmer decides.
  • Data gaps: missing data is shown as a gap, not a guess.
  • Accessibility: larger text, read aloud, less motion and high contrast.
  • Language: English/Spanish parity, checked by tests.
  • Digital literacy: two-tap answers and a guided tour.
  • Connectivity: mobile-first design and lazy loading.
  • Privacy: encryption and rate limiting.
  • Cost: operator switches pause AI, jobs, mail and push.
  • Seasons: the southern hemisphere is handled.
  • Responsible AI: daily caps, and the rule-based text stays when AI is off.
